metadata.title: Backpropagation, One Error at a Time
metadata.audience: makers and curious learners new to ML

beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. The ask: gradient descent needs a slope for every weight. How does a network get all of them at once? Show me backpropagation, with real numbers.

show.event: composer card fades in on cream
greeting 'Hola, Liam' types above the composer

props.segment: Backpropagation, One Error at a Time
props.command: Gradient descent needs a slope for every weight. How does a network get all of them at once? Show me backpropagation, with real numbers.
output: the trick: the chain rule, run backward from the error
worked example: one step drops the loss from 0.5245 to 0.0983
where it breaks: deep chains where the gradient fades away

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask lands answered; Liam introduced in first breath. Series link: film 1 (gradient descent) named backprop and moved on.

beats.narration_text: Backpropagation sends the error backward once. It doesn't test the weights one by one. It runs the chain rule from the loss back to the input, and every weight gets its slope.

show.event: 'tests every weight' turns terracotta, hesitates, backspaces

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — misconception corrected: backprop is not per-weight trial and error (finite differences); it is one backward pass of the chain rule.

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole network: four small steps in a row. Multiply by the first weight. Squash with tanh. Multiply by the second weight. Then score it: the loss is how far we land from the target, squared. Every step is simple, and every step has its own local slope. Backpropagation only ever needs those.

show.event: box '× w₁' → node z draws on
box '× w₂' → node y draws on
box '(y − t)²' → node L (loss) draws on
under each box, a small 'local slope' tag appears, one by one

shot.visual_intent: The network as a left-to-right chain of four simple operations, each with a local slope tag.
shot.motion_claim: The chain builds in narration order; the local-slope tags are the framework the film uses.

beats.narration_text: The chain rule says how a change in the first weight reaches the loss: multiply the local slopes along the path. How the loss moves with the output. How the output moves with h, which is the second weight. How tanh bends. And how z moves with the first weight, which is just the input. Four factors, one product.

show.event: box spotlight on ∂L/∂y; label 'how the loss moves with the output'
box on ∂y/∂h; label 'the second weight, w₂'
box on ∂h/∂z; label 'how tanh bends: 1 − h²'
all four factors underlined together: 'one product'

shot.visual_intent: The chain rule for w₁, factor by factor, each factor tied to a box in the B02 chain.
shot.motion_claim: The spotlight walks the factors right-to-left along the path the error travels.

beats.narration_text: Real numbers. Input one, target zero point two, weights zero point five and two. Forward: z is zero point five. Tanh gives zero point four six. Times two, the output is zero point nine two. We wanted zero point two, so the loss is about zero point five two. Now run it backward.

show.event: the B02 chain returns; x=1, t=0.2, w₁=0.5, w₂=2 tagged

shot.visual_intent: Forward pass: executed values fill each node left to right (demo/evidence.json).
shot.motion_claim: Each value lands as its node is spoken; the loss is the one accent.

beats.narration_text: Backward, the slopes multiply. The loss moves one point four five per unit of output. Times the second weight: two point nine. Times the tanh slope, zero point seven nine: two point two eight. That's the first weight's slope. The second weight's is zero point six seven. One step, step size zero point one, and the loss falls from zero point five two to just under zero point one.

show.event: terracotta arrows run right-to-left under the chain

shot.visual_intent: Backward pass: executed gradients flow right to left, then one update step.
shot.motion_claim: The multiplication is visible as the error travels; the loss counter drops on the spoken number.

beats.narration_text: Is that slope real? Check it the slow way: nudge the first weight up and down by a hundred-thousandth, and measure how the loss changes. Backprop says two point two seven eight three. The nudge says the same, to eight decimal places. But nudging costs two passes per weight. With a million weights, that's two million passes. Backprop needs one.

show.event: w₁ dial nudges ± 0.00001; two loss readings appear
cost bars: '2 passes per weight × 1,000,000' vs 'one backward pass'

shot.visual_intent: Finite-difference check against backprop, then the cost comparison that makes backprop matter.
shot.motion_claim: The two numbers sit side by side, digit-aligned; the cost bars grow on the spoken counts.

beats.narration_text: Here's where it bites. Stack ten sigmoid layers. A sigmoid's slope is never more than a quarter, so every layer multiplies the gradient by about zero point two two. By the time the error reaches the first layer, it's about three and a half ten-millionths. The early layers barely learn. That's the vanishing gradient, and it's one reason deep networks moved to ReLU.

show.event: ten sigmoid layers stack left to right
gradient bars shrink layer by layer, right to left (log scale)

shot.visual_intent: A deep sigmoid chain where the executed gradient shrinks by ~0.22 per layer.
shot.motion_claim: The bars visibly collapse as the error moves back; the tiny first-layer number is the accent.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Backprop runs the chain rule from the loss back to every weight. Each step only needs its own local slope, and slopes multiply along the path. One backward pass gives every weight its slope. A finite-difference check agrees, at far higher cost. And long chains of small slopes make gradients vanish.

show.event: verdict artifact card in on cream
lines 1–6 land on their spoken cue

artifactLines: Backprop runs the chain rule from the loss back to every weight.
Each step only needs its own local slope.
Slopes multiply along the path back to each weight.
One backward pass gives every weight its slope.
A finite-difference check agrees, at far higher cost.
Long chains of small slopes make gradients vanish.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a short Python script, no M L libraries, for y equals w two times tanh of w one times x, with loss y minus t, squared. Use x equals one, t equals zero point two, w one equals zero point five, w two equals two. Compute the slope of the loss for both weights with the chain rule, then check both with central finite differences, using a step of one hundred-thousandth. Print each pair and their difference. Then set w one to five, and explain, from the numbers, which factor in the chain shrinks the first weight's slope. Here's what to check. The first weight's slope should be about two point two eight, and match the finite difference. At w one equals five, watch the tanh slope collapse to almost nothing. And see whether Claude names the culprit: one minus tanh squared.

show.event: the prompt types into the composer
three check lines cascade in as each is spoken

props.command: Write a short Python script, no ML libraries, for y = w2 * tanh(w1 * x) with loss (y - t)^2, using x = 1, t = 0.2, w1 = 0.5, w2 = 2. Compute dL/dw1 and dL/dw2 with the chain rule, then check both with central finite differences using a step of 0.00001. Print each pair and their difference. Then set w1 = 5 and explain, from the numbers, which factor in the chain shrinks dL/dw1.
output: check: dL/dw1 ≈ 2.2783 and matches the finite difference
check: at w1 = 5 the tanh slope is about 0.0001816
check: it names 1 − tanh² as the factor that shrinks the gradient
